deck.title: IAM — Identity and Access Management
deck.analogy: AWS is a giant office building: users are employee badges, groups are departments, roles are temporary costumes, policies are the rules on the wall.

subtopics.title: How AWS decides yes or no
STS and roles: how the costume gets put on

cards.front: What is the difference between an IAM **user** and an IAM **role**?

back.answer: A user is a permanent identity with a password/long-lived keys; a role has no permanent credentials and is *assumed* to get temporary credentials.
back.explanation: Roles are used for services, cross-account access and federated humans.
back.mnemonic: User = employee badge; role = temporary costume.

cards.front: Can an IAM group contain other groups or roles?
An application on EC2 needs to write to DynamoDB. What's the MOST secure way to provide credentials?

back.answer: Attach an IAM role to the instance (instance profile).
back.explanation: The instance gets auto-rotating temporary credentials from metadata; no keys touch the disk.

choices.text: Create an IAM user and store its access keys in ~/.aws/credentials
choices.why: Long-lived keys on compute can leak and never rotate.

choices.text: Attach an IAM role via an instance profile
Bake access keys into the AMI
choices.why: Keys in AMIs are always wrong.

choices.text: Pass access keys as environment variables
choices.why: Still long-lived keys on the box.

cards.examTip: "MOST secure" + EC2 needs AWS access → instance role

cards.front: A user's policy clearly **Allows** an action, but it fails with Access Denied. What are the three usual causes?

back.answer: An explicit Deny somewhere, an SCP on the account, or a permission boundary.
back.explanation: Explicit Deny always wins; Allow + Deny = Deny.
